title: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting
outcomes: Spots loose pieces (attacked and not defended) on either side
Counts attackers and defenders of a square
Decides whether to start captures on a square by adding up the swaps, cheapest piece first

steps.text: A piece is **attacked** when an enemy piece could capture it. It is **defended** when a friendly piece could take back on that square. Attacked and **not defended** is **loose** here: it can be taken for free. Related words: **undefended** means no friendly piece guards it, even if nobody attacks it yet; **hanging** (*en prise*) means attacked without enough defence; **tactically vulnerable** means defended but still losable to a trick. Spot loose pieces, yours and theirs: the first safety habit.

steps.caption: The queen attacks the pawn on b6 and the bishop on d5. Only one of them is loose.

steps.text: When several pieces fight over one square, count. List the attackers and the defenders. Start captures with your cheapest attacker. Add up what each side takes and gives, and stop when the next swap would lose more than it wins. More attackers than defenders is not always enough.

steps.caption: Two attackers, one defender, and the pawn goes first. Count the swaps.

steps.title: Same count, different pieces
steps.prompt: Again two attackers and one defender. This time the target is a pawn and the first attacker is a knight. Predict first: does the count still win?
Pick one counting question. Which swap did you add up last, and did you check that each defender could really capture? Rate how sure you were of that answer. (low / medium / high)
